newsitem.title: USA: Democrat tops union's least-valuable director list.
newsitem.headline: Democrat tops union's least-valuable director list.

text.p: Tony Coelho, once the third highest ranking Democrat in the House, joined two former Republican-appointed officials atop the Teamsters Union's 1997 list of least valuable corporate directors.

The union's second annual study, issued Wednesday, ranked 19 corporate directors as least valuable, based on a rating system that reflects their other commitments, conflicts of interest and oversight of companies with poor performance.

"It's an effort to quantify performance," said Bartlett Naylor, director of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters Office of Corporate Affairs. "We're looking at it from the bottom instead of the top."

Coelho, a former California Democrat who was House Majority Whip when he resigned his seat in 1989 after acknowledging errors in financial disclosure reports, topped the least valuable list with 44 points.

Right behind him were former Defence Secretary Frank Carlucci with 42 points and former Secretary of State Lawrence Eagleburger with 40 points. Both served under Republican President Ronald Reagan in the 1980s.
"Everybody that appears on this year's list is somebody who serves on more than one board that has a serious problem," Naylor said.

An investor who bought $100 of stock on January 31, 1996, in the seven companies where Coelho was then a director would be stuck with shares worth only $79.80 a year later after stock prices climbed to record highs, the report said.

In the study, directors were given 15 points if they were on boards identified by compensation consultant Graef Crystal as awarding high pay to chief executives of low performing companies, five points for being on boards cited by the Council of Institutional Investors as having long-term stock market performance problems and five points for consulting at companies where they held directorships.

Five points were given for being on the board of a company that declared bankruptcy, three points for being on a board that was deemed to overpay itself relative to performance, three points for missing more than one-fourth of all board meetings, three points for being on a board that a Business Week magazine survey identified as one of America's worst and two points per board for serving on more than four boards.

Besides making the report public, the union will send the report to the trustees of its members' pension funds, which had assets of $59 billion before the recent selloff in the stock market, Naylor said.
"These directors are crucial," he said. "They are our agents overseeing the value of the company. And we want them to be real agents."

Other directors on the list include Wharton Business School Dean Thomas Garrity, Harvard Business School Professor Walter Salmon, former Time Inc. chairman Richard Munro and former Environmental Protection Agency chief William Ruckelshaus.

The report recommends that companies include shareholder-nominated directors on proxy cards along with the board's nominees, limit board service to no more than five per director and improve board member communication with individual shareholders.
